(I)
QUESTION  PRESENTED
Whether the courts  below were required, and failed,
to consider particular individualized aspects of petitioner’s illegal transportation of alcohol in order to reject
his claim that the Excessive Fines Clause entitles him
to avoid forfeiture of the instrumentality of that crime.

(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States

No. 25-246
KENNETH J. JOUPPI, PETITIONER
v.
STATE OF ALASKA

ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE SUPREME COURT OF ALASKA

BRIEF FOR THE UNITED STATES
AS AMICUS CURIAE SUPPORTING RESPONDENT

INTEREST OF THE UNITED STATES
This case concerns the interpretation  of the Eighth
Amendment’s Excessive Fines Clause.  The United States
has a substantial interest in that issue because it often
faces claims under the Clause when seeking fines under
federal law.
INTRODUCTION
From the founding era through the present day, it
has been commonplace to require forfeiture of the instrumentality of an illegal act —and, specifically, forfeiture of a vehicle used to unlawfully transport liquor .
The mandatory forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane, in
which he knowingly attempt ed to transport alcohol to a
dry Alaskan village, accords with that longstanding tradition.  It does not violate the Excessive Fines Clause.
Petitioner contends  (Br. 1) that a court should review
the excessiveness of that penalty “with reference to the

2

defendant’s own wrongdoing ,” and that his wrongdoing
does not justify the forfeiture because  he is a first -time
offender and only six of the 72 beers that he was transporting were in plain view.  But the forfeiture of the “instrument of the offence” is an “established” penalty,
Smith v. Maryland, 18 How. 71, 75 (1855), and t he
“time-honored” tradition of “[f ]orfeiture of vehicles”  for
alcohol smuggling  dates all the way back to the First
Congress , General Motors Acceptance Corp. v. United
States, 286 U.S. 49, 56 (1932).
Such forfeiture  has traditionally been mandatory, regardless of the value of the  instrumentality  or additional
details of the misconduct.  “Scales used to measure  out
unlawful  drug sales” are forfeitable “whether made of
the purest gold or the basest metal.”  Austin v. United
States, 509 U.S. 602, 627 (1993) (Scalia, J., concurring in
part and concurring in the judgment).  And even if that
history were not conclusive , the penalty was not
“grossly disproportional  to the gravity of the defendant’s offense,” particularly in light of the “  ‘substantial
deference ,’ ” United States  v. Bajakajian , 524 U.S. 321,
336-337 (1998) (citation omitted) , owed to the Alaska
legislature ’s considered judgment about the best way to
protect communities’ choices to  go completely dry to
prevent alcohol abuse  and its attendant social ills .
STATEMENT
1. The village of Beaver is  located on the north bank
of the Yukon River amidst the Yukon Flats, a vast wetland area in central Alaska.  See Valerie A. Sumida, Div.
of Subsistence, Alaska Dep’t of Fish & Game, Patterns
of Fish and Wildlife Harvest  and Use  in Beaver,
Alaska 7 (1989),  https://perma.cc/V7YB -82J9.  Beaver
was founded  in 1910, after the discovery of gold nearby ,
at the terminus of a trail linking the river to a mining

3

camp.  See id. at 7, 9.  When the gold rush ended, local
miners turned to trapping, and Beaver survived as a
trading post.  See id. at 9.  The village’s first post office
opened in 1913, followed by its first school in 1928.  See
ibid.
In the 2020 census, Beaver reported a population of
48.  See U.S. Census Bureau, Beaver CDP, Alaska ,
https://data.census.gov/all?g=160XX00US0205750 .  The
village is off the road system and is accessible primarily
by air.  See Sumida 9.  The nearest neighboring community, Fort Yukon, is about 60 miles away.  See ibid.
2. Remote Alaskan villages like Beaver face  serious
challenges  in addressing  the abuse of alcohol.  See Burnor v. State, 829 P.2d 837, 840 -841 (Alaska Ct. App.
1992).  The villages’ isolation, inaccessibility, and inclement weather make it difficult for police officers and medical personnel to respond to emergencies , increasing the
risks associated with alcohol abuse .  See ibid.
In 1980, f aced with studies showing that one in ten
Alaskans was an alcoholic, the state legislature  enacted
a local -option law.  See 1980 Alaska Sess. Laws ch. 131 ;
Harrison v. State, 687 P.2d 332, 335 -336 (Alaska Ct.
App. 1984).  As amended, that law allows a village to ban
the possession, sale, and importation  of alcohol.  See
Alaska Stat. § 04.11.491.  Beaver voted to go dry in a 2004
referendum  spurred by  an incident in which a 21 -yearold resident spent a night drinking, passed out outdoors
in sub-zero temperatures, and later choked to death on
his vomit.  See Joel Gay, Yukon River village backs prohibition , Fairbanks Daily News -Miner, Aug. 16, 2004.
3. Knowingly transporting or attempting  to trans -
port alcohol to a dry village  like Beaver is a crime under
Alaska state law .  See Alaska Stat. § 04.11.499.  While
the offense is  generally a misdemeanor,  it is a felony if

4

the offender  is a proven recidivist or the quantity of alcohol involved exceeds specified thresholds .  See id.
§ 04.16.200 (e).  Under either version, any “aircraft, vehicles, or vessels used to transport” alcohol to a dry village
are subject to forfeiture.  Id. § 04.16.220(a)(3).
State law  originally left trial courts with discretion
to decide whether to order such forfeitures,  see Pet.
App. 21a,  but in 2004, the legislature made  aircraft  forfeitures mandatory , see 2004 Alaska Sess. Laws ch. 124,
§ 11.  Although a conveyance is subject to forfeiture even
if someone other than the owner uses it to illegally
transport alcohol , an owner can reacquire the conveyance through remission  by showing, among other
things, that he was not a party to the crime and that he
did not know or have reason to believe that his property
would be used in violation of the law.  See Alaska Stat.
§ 04.16.220(e).
4. Petitioner operated  an air -taxi company, piloting
a small airplane that he owned and that his company
leased from him .  Pet. App. 3a-4a.  In April 2012, petitioner planned to fly a passenger from Fairbanks to
Beaver.  Id. at 4a.  After petitioner loaded the airplane,
state troopers who were investigating him for violating
the local -option alcohol laws stopped the airplane and
executed a search warrant .  Id. at 33a.  They found 72
cans (nine gallons)  of beer on board.  Id. at 4a, 24a, 33a.
Alaska charged petitioner with misdemeanor transportation of alcohol to a dry village.  Pet. App. 33a ; see
id. at 33a n.4 (explaining that the definition of
“transport” includes “ attempting  * * *  to deliver or
transfer”)  (emphasis omitted)  (quoting Alaska Stat.
§ 04.11.499( c)(3)).  The evidence at trial showed that at
least one six -pack of beer was in plain view to petitioner
when he loaded the airplane.  Id. at 4a.  A trooper  also

5

testified that petitioner would “have to be blind not to
know” that he had been loading beer on the airplane and
that “pilots with that bad of eyesight don’t fly.”  397 P.3d
1026, 1029.
The jury found petitioner guilty, and the trial court
sentenced him to 180 days in jail (wit h 177 days suspended), a fine of $3000 (with $1500 suspended), and
three years of probation.  Pet. App. 5a.  But the court
refused to order forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane,
which it valued at $95,000, on the view that such forfeiture would violate the  federal Constitution’s  Excessive
Fines Clause.  Id. at 163a; see id. at 152a-169a.
5. The Alaska Court of Appeals vacated and remanded after concluding  that the trial court’s legal
analysis and factual findings were incomplete.  Pet.
App. 30a -63a.  Judge Mannheimer filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part , in which he determined that forfeiture was “clearly proper.”  Id. at
65a; see id. at 64a-151a.
The Alaska Supreme Court vacated that judgment
and found that forfeiture  would be constitutional .  Pet.
App. 1a -29a.  The court found forfeiture not to be
grossly disproportiona te to petitioner’s crime because
petitioner had  “knowingly transported  a six-pack of alcohol in plain view while acting in his professional capacity as the operator of an air taxi company and the
pilot of the airplane ,” petitioner committed a “serious”
offense  by “knowingly” transporting alcohol to a dry village, petitioner was “clearly within the class” targeted
by the statute , the value of the plane was “only 9.5 times
the maximum fine ,” and the crime at issue causes
“grave societal harm.”  Id. at 19a-20a, 23a -24a.

6

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Our Nation has a long tradition, dating back to the
founding, of forfeiture of  the instrumentalities used to
commit crimes.  In accord with that tradition, t he Excessive Fines Clause allows the forfeiture of  the airplane that petitioner  knowingly  used to commit his
crime, regardless of the  value of the airplane or additional details of his misconduct .
A.  The tradition of instrumentality forfeitures includes a longstanding practice of forfeiting a conveyance used to smuggle alcohol.  The First Congress required the forfeiture of ships or carriages used to remove untaxed spirits from distilleries.  In 1834, Congress required the forfeiture of boats used to bring wine
or spirits into Indian country.  In the same month  that
the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified, Congress required the forfeiture of ships that smuggled spirits into
Alaska.  And during Prohibition, Congress  required the
forfeiture of vehicles involved in bootlegging .
Forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane fits within both
the general tradition of instrumentality forfeitures and
the more specific tradition of confiscating conveyances
used to smuggle alcohol.  Instrumentality f orfeiture s
traditionally did not depend on  the instrumentality’s
value.  Nor did they depend on additional details of the
offender’s misconduct , beyond the use of the conveyance.  And although the historical forfeitures were in
rem, they are closely analogous to  in personam  forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane .  Accordingly, historical
tradition  alone establishes that forfeiture  here complies
with the Excessive Fines Clause.
B.  Forfeiture here also passes muster under the
gross-disproportionality framework that this Court applied in United States v. Bajakajian , 524 U.S. 321

7

(1998), to evaluate the excessiveness of the forfeiture of
currency  that was the subject of a crime.  See id. at 336.
That standard requires a court to grant substantial deference to the legislature, which is responsible for determining the appropriate penalty for a crime in the first
instance.  See ibid.  The Alaska legislature did not exceed its broad authority here.
The Alaska legislature  has determined that the
transportation of alcohol to a dry village should result
in the mandatory forfeiture of the airplane used in the
crime, even if, as petitioner claims here, the offense involves a small quantity of alcohol.  Petitioner provides
no sound reason to disturb that  considered legislative
judgment.  While individualized circumstances can bear
on whether a mandatory f orfeiture is grossly disproportionate, the analysis must pay heed to  the severity of
the general problem that the legislature seeks to address and the specific role  of the forfeiture provision  in
responding to that problem .
The mandatory  penalty here embodies  the Alaska
legislature’s judgment that alcohol abuse poses a grave
problem in rural Alaska.  It reflects , among other things,
the difficulty of detecting alcohol smuggling : the harder
a crime is to catch, the stiffer a consequence  needs to be
to deter it.  And it directly addresses the a lcohol-
smuggling problem by eliminating the possibility that
airplanes used to smuggle alcohol will be used that way
again.  Petitioner is well within the heartland of  the statute.  The jury found that he knew that he was transporting alcohol, and even a small amount  of alcohol  can
cause substantial harms  in a community that has chosen
the all -in measure of banning alcohol completely.
C.  Petition er’s historical authorities, which concern
monetary fines, are inapposite because monetary fines

8

meaningfully differ from instrumentality forfeitures .
Judges historically had broad  discretion to determine
the amounts of monetary fines.  Such discretionary
fines raised concerns , like arbitrariness and deliberate
abuse, that are absent f or mandatory instrumentality
forfeitures , which target the instrumentalit ies selected
by the offender s themselves .  They also serve different
purposes; unlike a monetary fine, a forfeiture incapacitates an offender by depriving him of the instruments
of the offense.   Given those differences, courts should
analyze  instrumentality forfeitures under the historical
standards that govern those forfeitures, not under the
distinct standards that govern monetary fines.  And that
analysis confirms that forfeiture here is constitutional.
ARGUMENT
The Eighth Amendment provides  that “[e]xcessive
bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed,
nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted.”  U .S.
Const. Amend. VIII.   Where, as in the case of criminal
in personam  forfeiture here, forfeiture of property
“serves in part to punish,” it “can be a fine.”  Pung v.
Isabella County , 609 U.S. 30, 43  (2026) (brackets, citations and internal quotation marks omitted).  But history
conclusively  shows that, regardless of the other “particular facts” of the case, Pet. Br. 8 (citation omitted), forfeiture of the vehicle that petitioner knowingly  used in
the illegal  transportation of  alcohol—the instrumentality of his crime —is not excessive.  Nor, for that matter,
would forfeiture here be deemed excessive even under
the “gross disproportionality” standard that this Court
applied to a non -instrumentality forfeiture in United
States v. Bajakajian , 524 U.S. 321, 336 (1998) .

9

A. Forfeiture Of Petitioner’s Airplane Fits Within Our Nation’s Long Tradition Of Instrumentality Forfeitures
In applying the Excessive Fines Clause, this Court
has often begun by consulting historical practice.  See
Pung, 609 U.S. at 43; Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 336.  Here,
that practice shows that the government may confiscate
property that was used in serious crimes, including conveyances involved in alcohol smugg ling, regardless of
other details about the circumstances of the offense .
1. Our Nation has a long tradition of confiscating the
instrumentalities of crime, including  conveyances
involved in alcohol smuggling
a. For centurie s, legislatures have required  the forfeiture of instrumentalities of crime —i.e., property
used in the commission of offenses .  See Bajakajian ,
524 U.S. at 333 n.8.  Instrumentality  forfeitures began
in England more than seven centuries ago with the Statute of Westminster 1285, 13 Edw. 1, c. 47, which required forfeiture of  nets used for unlawful fishing .  Statutes enacted over the ensuing centuries similarly required the forfeiture of arms that were unlawfully carried in public, see Statute of Northampton  1328, 2 Edw.
3, c. 3 ; ships that were used for unlawful fishing, see
Fisheries, etc. Act 1663, 15 Car. 2, c. 16, § 2 ; and horses
and carriages that were used to carry unlawful exports,
see Wool Act 1695, 7 Will 3, c. 28, § 6.
The tradition crossed the Atlantic .  The Navigation
Acts, a series of seventeenth -century English laws regulating colonial trade, were enforced through  the forfeiture of ships involved in violations, and American  courts
routinely  conducted forfeiture proceedings under those
statutes .  See C.J. Hendry Co. v. Moore, 318 U.S. 133,
138-140 (1943).  Colonial legislatures also enacted their
own forfeiture laws, confiscating property ranging from

10

ships used to carry  unlawful exports, see Act of June 14,
1690, ch. 45, 1 Laws of New Hampshire 419 (Albert
Stillman Batchellor ed., 1904) , to guns used for poaching, see Act of Dec. 21, 1771, § 3, Laws of the State of
New-Jersey 26 (1821).
Forfeiture of instrumentalities remained common after independence.  The First Congress required  the forfeiture of ships, horses, and carriages involved in customs violations.  See, e.g., Collection Act of  1789, ch. 5,
§§ 12, 34, 40, 1 Stat. 39, 46, 48 -49; Collection Act of  1790,
ch. 35, §§ 14, 27, 60, 70, 1 Stat. 158, 163, 174, 177.  Later
in the 1790s, Congress required  the forfeiture of ships
involved in violating neutrality laws, slave-trade laws,
and embargos.  See, e.g., Slave Trade Act of  1794, ch.
11, § 1, 1 Stat. 349; Neutrality Act of  1794, ch. 50, § 3, 1
Stat. 383; Act of June 13, 1798, ch. 53, § 1, 1 Stat. 565.
And founding-era state legislatures provided for an
even broader range of forfeitures, including forfeitures
of “horses used in races that violated gambling laws,”
“shingles sold in bundles that violated commercial regulations,” and “gunpowder stored above the quantities
permitted by fire safety laws.”  Caleb Nelson, The Constitutionality of Civil Forfeiture , 125 Yale L.J. 2446,
2472 (2016) .
Instrumentality forfeitures remained routine in the
nineteenth century .  During the era surrounding ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment , for example,
Congress required  the forfeiture of tools used to manufacture untaxed goods, see Revenue Act of 1864, ch. 173,
§ 48, 13 Stat. 240; railway cars  used to smuggle  imports,
see Smuggling Act of  1866, ch. 201, § 3, 14 Stat. 178-179;
and vessels used to hunt  endangered seals in Alaska,
see Act of July 27, 1868, ch. 273, § 6, 15 Stat. 241.  And
instrumentality forfeitures remain commonplace t oday,

11

including forfeitures of aircraft and other conveyances
used to transport illegal drugs, see 21 U.S.C. 881(a)(4) ,
equipment used in copyright piracy, see 18 U.S.C.
2323(a)(1)(B) , and unlawfully possessed firearms, see 18
U.S.C. 922(d)(1).
b. The Nation has not only a general tradition  of confiscating instrumentalities  of crime, but also a more specific historical practice  of confiscating conveyances used
to illegally  transport alcohol.  At the federal level , that
practice  began with the First Congress, which required
the forfeiture of ships, horses, and carriages used to remove untaxed spirits from distilleries.  See Whiskey
Tax Act of 1791, ch. 15, § 19, 1 Stat. 204 .  Discussing  that
statute in a report to the Second Congress, Secretary of
the Treasury Alexander Hamilton explained  that the
“forfeiture of the ship or vessel, and of the wa ggon or
other instrument of conveyance, assistant in a breach of
the law,” was a “common” and “comparatively  moderate” “penalt[y]”  that “cannot truly be deemed either unusual or excessive.”  11 The Papers of Alexander Hamilton 82-83 (Harold C. Syrett et al. eds. , 1966).
The practice of forfeiture of  the instrumentalities of
crime continued during the nineteenth  century.  In the
1820s, New Jersey and Pennsylvania  required forfeiture of many types of  conveyance s involved in the crime
of selling liquor near a place of worship .  See Act of Feb.
2, 1820, § 2, 1820 N.J. Acts 41; Act of Apr. 2, 1822,  ch.
169, § 2, 1822 Pa. Acts 287.   In 1834, Congress required
the forfeiture of boats used in bringing wine or spirits
into Indian country, and in 1864, it extended that provision to wagons and sleds.  See Trade and Intercourse
Act of 1834, ch. 161, § 20, 4 Stat. 732; Act of Mar. 15,
1864, ch. 33, 13 Stat. 29.  Those statutes, this Court has
remarked , show that “severe penalties” for bringing  liq-

12

uor in to Indian country date to “an early period of our
history.”  United States v. McGowan, 302 U.S. 535, 538
(1938).  Later, in the same month  when the Fourteenth
Amendment was ratified, Congress required the forfeiture of any “vehicle or animal used in carrying or conveying” spirits from an unlawful  distillery , see Act of
July 20, 1868,  ch. 186,  § 18, 15 Stat. 132 , as well as  any
ship that smuggled spirits worth more than $400 into
the newly acquired territory of Alaska , see Act of July
27, 1868, § 4, 15 Stat. 241.
Legislatures in the early twentieth century extended
the instrumentality -forfeiture  practice to cars and airplanes.  During Prohibition,  Congress required  the forfeiture of any “vehicle,” including  any “air craft,” used
to transport  liquor.  Volstead Act, ch. 85, Tit. II, § 26, 41
Stat. 315.   States generally  included similar  forfeiture
provisions in their own prohibition laws.  See Kenneth
A. Murchison, Property Forfeiture in the Era of National Prohibition , 32 Buff. L. Rev. 417, 423 & n.24
(1983).  And after the Twenty -First Amendment ended
national Prohibition , Congress required  the forfeiture
of any “vehicle” —including any  “means of transportation  * * *  through the air” —used to bring liquor into a
dry State.  Liquor Enforcement Act of 1936, ch. 815,
§§ 2(b), 4, 49 Stat. 1928.
The practice has endured to the present .  Federal
law today requires the forfeiture of “every vehicle ,” including any “means of transportation  *  * *  through the
air,” used to transport liquor in violation of federal commercial regulations.  18 U.S.C. 3667.  It also requires the
forfeiture of “[a]ny conveyance” used to introduce liquor “into the Indian country, or into other places where
the introduction is prohibited by treaty or enactment of
Congress.”  18 U.S.C. 3669.

13

2. Forfeiture  of an instrumentality traditionally does
not depend on the relation between its value and the
offender’s conduct
Historical practice shows that the “unlawful use” of
property is generally a sufficient basis for confiscating
it.  Austin v. United States , 509 U.S. 602, 627 (1993)
(Scalia, J., concurring in part and concurring in the
judgment).  Forfeiture  of an instrumentality of a crime
does not depend on an assessment  of the value of the
property or the relation between that value and the offender’s conduct.
a. Traditionally, “the value of the property [used in
a crime] is irrelevant to whether it is forfeited.”  Austin,
509 U.S. at 62 6 (Scalia, J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment).  At the founding , a vessel involved in a customs violation was forfeited  whether it
was a boat or a three -masted ship.  See Kevin Arlyck,
The Founders’ Forfeiture , 119 Colum. L. Rev. 1449,
1475 (2019).  During Prohibition , a vehicle used to
transport liquor was forfeited  whether it was a “wheelbarrow” or a “Rolls Royce.”  United States v. One 1936
Model Ford V -8 Deluxe Coach , 307 U.S. 219, 237 (1939).
Today, a defendant is not entitled to special protection
from forfeiture simply because he chooses to use a Lamborghini, rather than a beat -up old jalopy, to transport
drugs.  I n other words , “[s]cales used to measure out
unlawful drug sales” are forfeitable  “whether made of
the purest gold or the basest metal.”  Austin, 509 U.S.
at 627 (Scalia, J., concurring in part and concurring in
the judgment).
That tradition reflects a core purpose of forfeiture:
depriving offenders “of the instruments through which
they might commit further crimes.”  United States v.
Cullen, 979 F.2d 992, 994 (4th Cir. 1992).  “ Forfeiture of

14

conveyances that have been used —and may be used
again—in violation of the ” law “prevent[s] further illicit
use of the conveyance. ”  Calero-Toledo v. Pearson Yacht
Leasing Co. , 416 U.S. 663, 686-687 (1974).   That objective has nothing to do with the value of the property .
“So far as the public welfare is concerned, the Ferrari
[used to carry drugs] is at least as harmful an instrumentality as the Chevette.”  Cullen, 979 F.2d at 99 5.  If
anything , property may be more valuable precisely because of features that make it more useful in crime —
say, a “$14 million yacht, specially outfitted with high -
powered motors, radar, and secret compartments for
the sole purpose of transporting drugs.”  United States
v. Chandler , 36 F.3d 358, 364 (4th Cir. 1994) , cert. denied, 514 U.S. 1082 (1995) .
b. Forfeiture likewise  does not depend on the details
of the offender’s conduct beyond the use of the conveyance.  The historical laws discussed above did not make
the propriety of instrumentality forfeitures contingent
on an “ ‘individualized assessment ’ ” of the “the defendant’s own wrongdoing. ”  Pet. Br. 2, 34 (citation omitted).
Nor did they leave the forfeiture to the discretion of the
court.  Instead, they provided  that anyone who commits
a given crime would forfeit a given instrumentality .
For instance, certain founding-era customs violations,
such as importing liquor in casks of the wrong size or
bearing the wrong marks, resulted in the mandatory
forfeiture of the ship , even if the  government  lost only
a few dollars in revenue  and even if the ship was worth
thousands .  See Arlyck 1474 -1475.  In one case from
1795, a shipowner brought on board two casks of rum to
sell to passengers traveling from Ireland to New York.
See id. at 1475.  Because the casks bore the wrong
marks, t he government sought forfeiture of the $12,000

15

ship—“a penalty more than 100 times greater than the
duties owed” on the rum.  Ibid.  Other cases from the
1790s involved the forfeiture of an $11,5 50 ship for importing undersized casks containing beer worth $87.50;
the forfeiture of a $6000 ship for importing undersized
casks containing beer worth $240; and the forfeiture of
a $2000 ship for importing undersized casks containing
gin worth $14.84.  See id. at 1475 n.155.
At most, early statutes accounted for the owner’s
mens rea , or the “overwhelming necessity” of the conduct.  Culley v. Marshall, 601 U.S. 377, 400 (2024) (Gorsuch, J., concurring)  (citation omitted) .  Some statutes
allowed an owner to  avoid forfeiture by showing that the
violation “proceeded from accident or mistake.”  Collection Act of 1799, ch. 22, §  67, 1 Stat. 677.  Others gave
the Secretary of the Treasury discretion to grant relief
if the owner’s culpability did not rise to the level of “wilful negligence.”  Remission Act of 1790, ch. 12, § 1, 1
Stat. 123.  And in the absence of express statutory language, courts construed forfeiture statutes to apply
only if the property was misused with the “consent or
connivance” of the owner or of “some person employed
or trusted by him.”  Peisch v. Ware, 4 Cranch 347, 364
(1808) (Marshall, C.J.).  Those limited practices, however, stopped far short of  a freewheeling  inquiry into
other individual  circumstances .
3. Because forfeiture here comports  with historical
practice, it is not excessive
a. The Alaska State Legislature has made the judgment that  the transportation of alcohol to a dry village
should be addressed , in part, by forfeiture of the “aircraft, vehicles, or vessels used” in the crime.  Alaska
Stat. § 04.16.220(a)(3).  The state legislature at first
made such forfeitures  discretionary , but it determined

16

in 2004 that alcohol smuggling  by air is such a serious
problem that aircraft forfeitures should be mandatory.
See 2004 Alaska Sess. Laws ch. 124, § 11.
Because an airplane used to fly alcohol to a dry village is unquestionably an instrumentality —i.e., the
“means by which an offense [i]s committed,” Bajakajian , 524 U.S. at 333 n.8 —its forfeiture fits within
the general tradition of confiscating criminal instrumentalities.  More specifically, t he forfeiture carries on
the tradition of confiscating conveyances used to unlawfully transport alcohol.  Petitioner emphasizes (Br. 39)
that his airplane is worth $95,000, but history shows
that a conveyance used to transport alcohol is forfeitable whether it is a snowmobile or a luxury je t.
If anything, the forfeiture here is more moderate
than others that have historically been permitted.   Traditionally, an owner could forfeit his property because
someone else  “employed or trusted” by him used it to
commit a crime.  Peisch, 4 Cranch  at 364.  This Court
has recognized, for instance, that an owner may forfeit
a ship because the crew uses it for piracy, see Harmony
v. United States , 2 How. 210, 234 (1844); that a landlord
may forfeit a building because a lessee uses to run an
illegal distillery, see Dobbins’s Distillery v. United
States, 96 U.S. 395, 399 (1878); and that a leasing company may forfeit a yacht because a lessee uses it to
transport marijuana, see Calero-Toledo, 416 U.S. at
690.  A fortiori , a State may confiscate an airplane that
the owner himself knowingly uses in a crime.
To the extent that history sometimes permitted an
exception for an owner who was merely negligent, or
who undertook  an illegal act due to necessity, no such
exception  is at issue here.  Petitioner’s crime did not result from mere accident, inadvertence, or negligence, or

17

from someone else’s use of his airplane without his consent or connivance.  The jury instead found petitioner
guilty of knowingly using his own airplane to violate the
law.  See Pet. App. 5a.  And he does not claim that it was
necessary to fly Budweiser to  Beaver.
b. The forfeiture in this case differs in one respect
from its for ebears: it was collected in an in personam
criminal prosecution against petitioner , s ee Pet. App.
14a, while historical instrumentality forfeitures were
collected through in rem  civil proceedings directed at
the property, see Bajakajian , 524 U.S. at 329 -332.  The
Court has stated that in rem forfeitures, including at
least some instrumentality forfeitures, “were considered to occupy a place outside the domain of the Excessive Fines Clause” because they were “directed against
‘guilty property’  ” and were “not considered punishment
against the individual .”  Id. at 330 -331.  But the Court
has also recognized that “statutory in rem forfeiture
* * *  historically  ha[s] been understood, at least in part,
as punishment” for “the owner.”  Austin, 509 U.S. at
618.  And the in rem/in personam  distinction makes no
difference here .
As Justice Story recognized  nearly two hundred
years ago , even if historical “laws providing for in rem
forfeiture of goods imported in violation of customs
laws” “  ‘truly deserve [d] to be called, remedial,’  ” they
“in one sense ‘impose[d] a penalty. ’ ”  Bajakajian , 524
U.S. at 331 (quoting Taylor v. United States , 3 How.
197, 210 (1845)).  Laws that required the forfeiture of
the instrumentalities  used to transport such goods had
an evident  (albeit latent) penal aspect.  Although s uch
laws “ascrib[ed] to the property a certain personality,”
that anthropomorphism could not alone explain them.
J.W. Goldsmith, Jr. -Grant Co. v. United States , 254

18

U.S. 505, 510 (1921).   “To th [at] superstitious reason ,”
“Blackstone add [ed] ‘that such misfortunes are in part
owing to the negligence of the owner and therefore, he
is properly punished by such forfeiture.’  ”  Ibid. (emphasis added) ); see 1  William Blackstone , Commentaries on the Laws of England  291 (1765) ; see also
Calero-Toledo, 416 U.S. at 686 .  As contemporaneous
observers , including Chief Justice Marshall,  were well
aware, “inanimate matter can commit no offence,” and
the “mere wood, iron, and sails of the ship, cannot, of
themselves, violate the law.”  United States v. The Little
Charles , 26 F. Cas. 979, 982 (C.C.D. Va. 1818) (No.
15,162) (Marshall, C.J.) ; see Beth A. Colgan, Of Guilty
Property and Civil/Remedial Punishment , 3 J. Am.
Const. Hist. 697, 712 -739 (2025).
Because historical in rem instrumentality  forfeitures
served at least in part to punish, they  are closely analogous to  the punitive  in personam  forfeiture here .  A
well-established penalty does not become  excessive—
i.e., “surpassing the usual, the proper, or a normal measure of proportion,” Bajakajian , 524 U.S. at 335 —just
because the State chooses to collect it in personam  rather than in rem.
c. To the extent that petitioner might contend that
this Court’s decision in Bajakajian requires that the
Court simply ignore the volumes of history that support
forfeiture in this case, such a contention would be misplaced.  Bajakajian did not itself involve an instrumentality forfeiture, but instead an in personam  forfeiture
of the  “subject of the crime”: the  entire $357,144 that
the defendant was carrying, for failing to report that he
was transporting more than $10,000 out of the country.
524 U.S. at 334 n.9 ; see ibid. (“The currency in question
is not an instrumentality.”) .  The Court’s analysis was

19

divided into two parts, the first of which does not implicate any issue disputed in this case, and the second of
which does not address whether historical in rem instrumentality forfeitures  are relevant to the constitutionality of modern in personam  ones.
The first part of the Bajakajian ’s analysis concerned
whether  the in personam  forfeiture there should be
deemed a “fine,” subject to the Excessive Fines Clause,
because it “constitute[d] punishment.” 524 U.S. at 330 -
334.  In the course of that analysis, the Court suggested
that at least some “traditional civil in rem forfeitures,”
including at least some instrumentality forfeitures,
were “inapposite” to the classification of modern criminal forfeitures as fines  “because such [ in rem ] forfeitures were historically considered nonpunitive.  Id. at
330.  The Court observed that the “theory behind” those
in rem  forfeitures “was the fiction that the action was
directed against ‘guilty property,’ rather than against
the offender himself ,” id. at 330 , and deemed that distinction insufficient to support the classification of modern criminal forfeitures —whether of goods or instrumentalities —as nonpunitive, id. at 333-334.  It is accordingly uncontested that the in personam  forfeiture here
should be treated as a fine.
The second part of the Court’s analysis, which undertook a proportionality determination, did not dismiss
traditional in rem  forfeitures out of hand.  To the contrary, it considered at length the government’s “contention that the proportionality of full forfeiture is demonstrated by the fact that the First Congress enacted statutes requiring full forfeiture of goods involved in customs offenses or the payment of moneta ry penalties
proportioned to the goods’ value.”  Bajakajian , 524 U.S.
at 340; see id. at 340-344.  The Court’s  rationale for re-

20

jecting the comparison did not rest solely on the in rem
nature of the historical proceedings, but instead on the
purpose that the historical forfeitures were meant to
serve.  Unlike the forfeiture of the entire $357,144 that
the defendant in Bajakajian  was carrying, the early
“goods” forfeitures “sought to vindicate the Government’s underlying property right in customs duties,” id.
at 34 0, or “serv[ed] the remedial purpose of reimbursing the Government for the losses accruing from the
evasion of customs duties,” id. at 342.  And a monetary
exaction “that serves purely remedial purposes cannot
be considered ‘excessive.’  ”  Austin, 509 U.S. at 622 n.14.
The traditional instrumentality forfeiture s here,
however, cannot be characterized simply as “remedies”
for violating customs laws.  Some of them were not attached to customs (or tax) laws  at all , but were instead
directed at the instrumentalities of other types of  forbidden activities.  See, e.g., Nelson 2472 (describing forfeitures for gambling and unsafe gunpowder storage).
And even the revenue -related ones  were not directed at
government losses.  Instead, as explained above, see p.
17-18, supra, they had latent penal objectives .  It is
clear from their very nature, and the manner in which
they were applied, that they were calibrated not to the
amount of the government’s loss (or presumed loss), but
instead to serve the purposes of “preventing further illicit use ” and “ imposing an economic penalty, thereby
rendering illegal behavior unprofitable .”  Calero-Toledo,
416 U.S. at 687 ; see United States v. The Brig Burdett ,
9 Pet. 682, 690 (1835) (“forfeiture of the vessel  *  * *  for
a violation of a revenue law  * * *  is  * * *  highly penal”).
Nothing in Bajakajian compels a court to willfully
blind itself to the historical tradition  of considering instrumentality forfeitures an appropriate response to

21

the use of property —of whatever value —to violate the
law.  While Bajakajian  noted that some “early customs
statutes”  required forfeiture not just of “goods” but of
“the vessels carrying them as well ,” its analysis focused
exclusively on the goods .  524 U.S. a t 340 (citing only
examples involving forfeiture of “goods”) .  That is presumably because the Court considered the only possible
analogue for the defendant’s “[c]ash in a suitcase”  to be
smuggled goods that are likewise the “subject of the
crime.”  Id. at 334 n.9.  Th e airplane here, however, is
an “instrumentality” of a crime, like “an automobile” or
ship that “facilitates the transportation of goods concealed to avoid taxes,” ibid., and appropriately evaluated
in light of the history of similar forfeitures.
B. Forfeiture Of Petitioner’s Airplane Also Satisfies  General Standards Of Proportionality
While h istory provides a sufficient basis for the forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane , the forfeiture  would also
be valid under the general proportionality  standard  applied in  Bajakajian .  See 524 U.S. at 33 4-344.  That
standard draws guidance from  the Court’s “Cruel and
Unusual Punishments Clause precedents,” and requires
only avoiding  “gross” disproportionality, not  achieving
“strict” proportionality.  Id. at 336.  Accordingly, it is satisfied so long  as the  fine “bear[s] some relationship to
the gravity of the offense that it is designed to punish.”
Id. at 334.   And i n making that assessment, the prescribed amount of the fine receives “  ‘substantial deference,’ ” because “judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the
legislature .”  Id. at 336 ( quoting Solem v. Helm, 463
U.S. 277, 290 (1983)).   There is no sound basis to reject
the Alaska legislature’s judgment here.

22

1. Proportionality review of a mandatory forfeiture  requires that any individualized circumstances be
viewed in light of systemic legislative objectives
As described in Bajakajian , the excessiveness  inquiry “must compare the amount of the forfeiture to the
gravity of the defendant ’s offense.  If the amount of the
forfeiture is grossly disproportional to the gravity of the
defendant ’s offense, it is unconstitutional. ”  Bajakajian ,
524 U.S. at 336-337.  That deferential standard recognizes both “ ‘the broad authority that legislatures necessarily possess in determining the types and limits of
punishments for crimes’ ” and  the “inheren [t] imprecis[ion]” of “judi cial determination regarding the gravity” of an offense.   Id. at 336 (citation omitted) .  Accordingly, while individualized circumstances of an offender’s
conduct can be relevant, their relevance and weight
must be considered in relation to the legitimate legislative objectives of a penalty—especially a mandatory one.
a. The legislature here prescribed a mandatory penalty, requiring forfeiture of any “aircraf t” “ used to
transport” alcohol to a dry village.  See Alaska Stat.
§§ 04.16.220(a)(3)  and (i).  As the Court’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause precedents recognize, legislatures may choose mandatory, determinate sentences
rather than  discretionary, individualized sentences.
See Harmelin v. Michigan, 501 U.S. 957, 994-996 (1991);
Chapman v. United States , 500 U.S. 453, 466-467 (1991).
Indeed, determinate sentencing was  the norm for death
or term -of-years sentences at the founding; individualized sentencing is largely a  more modern development.
See United States v. Grayson, 438 U.S. 41, 45-46 (1978).
The Court’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause
precedents also emphasize  that proportionality review
requires “a comprehension of all that the legislature did

23

or could take into account,  that is, a consideration of the
mischief and the remedy. ”  Weems v. United States , 217
U.S. 349, 379 (1910).  The Court has accordingly upheld
a mandatory sentence of life in prison without parole for
possessing 672 grams of cocaine in large part because
“drugs represent ‘one of the greatest problems affecting the health and welfare of our population.’  ” Harmelin, 501 U.S. at 1002 (Kennedy, J., concurring in part
and concurring in the judgment) (citation omitted).  The
Court has also upheld a mandatory sentence of 25 years
to life in prison for a recidivist felon, even though his
most recent conviction was for stealing three golf clubs,
largely because “[r]ecidivism is a serious public safety
concern.”  Ewing v. California , 538 U.S. 11, 26 (2003)
(plurality opinion).
b. While Bajakajian demonstrates that “the gravity
of the defendant’s offense ” is relevant to the proportionality of a mandatory forfeiture, 524 U.S. at 337, giving
significant weight to individual circumstances when reviewing the proportionality of a mandatory penalty
would subvert the principle that a “sentencing scheme
providing for ‘individualized sentences rests not on constitutional commands, but on public  policy enacted into
statutes.’  ”  Chapman, 500 U.S. at 467 ; see Bajakajian ,
524 U.S. at 325 (statute required full forfeiture of all unreported currency) .  The relevance of individual circumstances will depend , in particular,  on what the forfeiture
is intended to accomplish .  See Ewing, 538 U.S. at 29
(“[P]roportionality review  *  * *  must take [the penalty’s] goal into account.” ); 4 Blackstone 12 (1769)
(“[P]unishment ought always to be proportioned to the
particular purpose it means to serve .”).
In Bajakajian , for example, the government asserted a “correlation between the amount forfeited and

24

the harm that the Government would have suffered had
the crime” of unreported currency transportation  “gone
undetected.”   524 U.S. at 339.  But other types of mandatory f orfeiture s may have other goals .  Here, for example, the Alaska legislature made a specific judgment
that “aircraft” used to transport alcohol to a dry community should be forfeited.  Alaska Stat. § 04.16.220(a)(3).
One obvious goal of requiring forfeiture of that specific
instrumentality is  to eliminate the possibility that the
aircraft  will be used for additional alcohol  smuggling.
See Calero-Toledo, 416 U.S. at 687.   Individual circumstances may be more or less relevant to those or other
particular “mischief  [s]” and “remed[ies] ,” Weems, 217
U.S. at 379 , that are the subject of the legislation.
2. Forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane is not grossly disproportionate to his offense
Applying those principles  to the circumstances of
this case, forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane was not
grossly disproportionate to his offense.   The penalty is
substantial , but so is the problem that the penalty aimed
to address.  And petitioner’s conduct was not so innocuous as to support a constitutional exemption from the
Alaska legislature’s judgment.
a. The legislature  enacted the local-option law in
1980 after considering  studies showing that one in ten
Alaskans was an alcoholic,  that Alaska’s alcoholism
mortality rate was more than four times the national average, and that alcohol consumption in Alaska had risen
at twice the national rate.  See Harrison v. State, 687
P.2d 332, 335 (Alaska Ct. App. 1984).  The legislature
also found that “the dangers resulting from alcohol
abuse are particularly acute in rural areas of the state
because the communities are small, isolated, without
adequate law enforcement, without adequate health

25

care facilities, and populated by people who are closely
related and interdependent.”  1986 Alaska Sess. Laws
ch. 80, § 1 (6).
Such rural areas —including Beaver —may be unreachable by means other than airplanes or other specialized vehicle s, making it particularly important that
the operators of such vehicles respect the State’s dry
laws and the local community’s uncompromising effort
to avoid the possibility of alcohol abuse.  Forfeiture of
petitioner’s airplane ensures that the plane will not be
used in the future to violate Beaver’s, or some other
community’s,  considered choice to live alcohol -free.  The
other penalties attached to the crime confirm the appropriateness of the penalty.  Petitioner faced a maximum
of one year of imprisonment, see Pet. App. 34a —a term
significant enough to trigger the right to trial by jury,
see Blanton v. North Las Vegas , 489 U.S. 538, 542
(1989).  His air -taxi company, which was not subject to
jail time, faced a maximum fine of $500,000, see Pet. App.
7a n.10—more than five times the value of the airplane.
The severity of the penalty also reflects the difficulty
of detecting petitioner’s crime.  “Alaska has always
been a vast and thinly populated region where it is difficult for law enforcement officers to detect and prevent
smuggling.”  Pet. App. 77a (Mannheimer, J., concurring
in part and dissenting in part).  “[S]ince deterrent effect
depends not only upon the amount of the penalty but
upon its certainty, ” a crime that is “ less grave but significantly more difficult to detect”  often warrants “substantially higher penalties.”  Harmelin , 501 U.S. at 989
(opinion of Scalia, J.).   Nor is petitioner an innocent
owner.  Although Alaska law would allow forfeiture for
merely negligent conduct, the jury here found that petitioner knowingly used his own airplane to violate the

26

law.  See Pet. App . 5a.  That in itself raises at least the
possibility of prior undetected conduct , as well as the
possibility of its continuation.
Finally,  as discussed above,  the forfeiture here  bears
the endorsement  of history.  See pp. 9-21, supra.  Even
if history is not dispositive, a court should hesitate to
conclude that a consequence  as old as the Republic —the
forfeiture of a conveyance involved in smuggling —is
grossly disproportionate.
b. Petitioner argues (Br. 1-2) that the forfeiture was
excessive because  he was a first -time offender and was
(he says)  aware of only the six beers that were clearly
visible to him, not all 72 beers on the airplane.  See Pet.
App. 24a -25a.  But Alaska’s statutory scheme  embodies
a considered legislative determination  that the types of
facts that petitioner emphasizes —the quantity of alcohol and lack of a prior record —should not affect forfeiture of an aircraft .  Particularly because “ any judicial
determination regarding the gravity of a particular
criminal offense will be inherently imprecise ,” Bajakajian , 524 U.S. at 336,  petitioner presents no sound
reason to substitute an amorphous judicial line-drawing
exercise in place of the Alaska legislature’s considered
judgment.
Alaska distinguishes between misdemeanor and felony transportation of alcohol based on how much alcohol
is involved and whether the offender has a prior record,
see Alaska Stat. § 04.16.200(e), but it has made  aircraft
forfeiture mandatory even for the misdemeanor, see id.
§ 04.16.220(a)(3)(C).  Further, while Alaska has made
forfeiture of aircraft mandatory across the board, it has
required forfeiture of vehicles or watercraft only when
the offender has a prior record or the quantity of alcohol
exceeds specified thresholds .  See id. § 04.16.220(i).  Ve-

27

hicle and watercraft forfeitures , but not aircraft forfeitures, are also subject to an exception for cases where
“the vehicle or watercraft is the sole means of transportation for a family.”  Id. § 04.16.220(  j)(1).  That design
shows that the legislature viewed “aircraft -facilitated
importation as more severe than other methods of unlawful importation .”  Pet. App. 22a.   Even if an airplane
owner has never been caught before, the airplane is
what enabled the crime ( as well as any  past undiscovered and possible future crimes).  And even assuming
that a six -pack would not  itself cause drunkenness in  a
Beaver resident un accustomed  to alcohol, it could have
other ill effects, such as whetting a recovering alcoholic’s taste for liquor.  A community’s decision to be
completely dry is not a half -measure.
c. Any comparison between the circumstances here
and the circumstances in Bajakajian , which found forfeiture of the entire $357,144  to be excessive, is inapt.
This case involves a more precise, more squarely applicable legislative judgment than Bajakajian : forfeiture
not of the amount of currency that  the violator of a reporting requirement  happened to be carrying, but  of an
airplane that, whatever its value, was used  and is capable of being used again  to illegally transport alcohol.
The defendant in Bajakajian  also “d[id] not fit into
the class of persons for whom the statute was principally designed .”  524 U.S. at 338.  “He [was] not a money
launderer, a drug trafficker, or a tax evader ,” but instead planned to use the currency “to repay a lawful
debt.”  Ibid.  Here, in contrast, the Alaska judiciary has
made clear  that “a pilot knowingly transporting a passenger’s alcohol to a dry village is precisely the kind of
person and conduct that  the legislature was concerned
about.”  Pet. App. 26a.  The Alaska legislature  has ac-

28

cordingly required the forfeiture of an airplane that was
used to engage in substantive conduct that, in the legislature’s judgment, threatens serious societal harm.
C. Petitioner’s Near-Exclusive Reliance On Cases Involving Fines, Rather Than Instrumentality Forfeitures, Is
Misplaced
Petitioner relies almost exclusively ( Br. 20-32) on the
history of monetary fines  in arguing that  the forfeiture
of his airplane is excessive .  But this case involves an
instrumentality forfeiture, not a monetary fine.  Given
the historical and functional differences between such
penalties, the “excessiveness analysis” for instrumentality forfeitures “must be different from that applicable to monetary fines.”  Austin, 509 U.S. at 627 (Scalia,
J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment).
Historically, amounts of monetary fines were  usually
left to the discretion of courts .  B lackstone wrote that,
because the “value of money ” changes and because
“what is ruin to one man’s fortune, may be  [a] matter of
indifference to another’s,” the amounts of “pecuniary
fines” could not be “ascertained by any invariable law.”
4 Blackstone 371.  Such fines accordingly  pose risks of
abuse that mandatory instrumentality forfeitures do not.
For example, the English Bill of Rights’ excessive -
fines provision , from which our Excessive Fines Clause
descends, was adopted largely in response to the  Stuart
kings’ use of exorbitant fines to target parliamentary
critics and religious dissidents.  See Timbs v. Indiana,
586 U.S. 146, 152 (2019).  One member of Parliament
complained that “Men have been fined, not according to
their Crimes, but their Principles: Sometimes because
they have been Protestants.”  8 Debates of the House of
Commons, From the Year 1667 to the Year 1694 , at 228
(Anchitell Grey ed., 1763) .  In contrast,  prosecutors  and

29

courts do not control the amount of an instrumentality
forfeiture , so they cannot increase that amount based
on the offender’s  identity.
By the same token, m onetary fines , but not instrumentality forfeitures,  are capable of causing “a shock to
the offender who learns the severity of his sentence only
after he commits the crime .”  Harmelin , 501 U.S. at
1008 (Kennedy, J., concurring in part and concurring in
the judgment) .  To take one of petitioner’s examples (at
26-27), when the Earl of Devonshire assaulted Thomas
Culpeper in 1687, he had no way to anticipate that a
court would fine him £30,000.  Instrumentality -forfeiture
laws, however, provide clear warning: if you use something to commit a crime, then that thing will be  forfeited.  An offender who knowingly uses a valuable asset
in his offense has only  himself to blame for the value of
the forfeiture .
The potential for a fine beyond a defendant’s means
has also historically led to abuse s that have no analogue
in an instrumentality forfeiture .  In England, offenders
could be jailed until they paid their fines, prompting
Blackstone to remark that  “fines in the king’s court are
frequently denominated ransoms” and that  “a stated
imprisonment” “is better than an excessive fine, for that
amounts to imprisonment for life.”  4  Blackstone 373.
Similarly, after  the Civil War, southern States imposed
draconian fines for violations of the Black Codes  and demanded involuntary labor from those who could not pay.
See Timbs, 586 U.S. at 153.  Instrumentality forfeitures
do not raise such concerns , “for of necessity the [property] is there to satisfy the forfeiture.”  Bajakajian , 524
U.S. at 355 (Kennedy, J., dissenting ).
Finally, the penalties pursue different objectives .
Monetary fines generally seek retribution and deter-

30

rence.  See Cooper Industries, Inc. v. Leatherman Tool
Group, Inc. , 532 U.S. 424, 432 (2001).  But they do not
have the same incapacitative rationale as instrumentality
forfeitures, which “remov[e] the instrument [s] through
which” the law has been violated .  Cullen, 979 F.2d at
994.  Even if a $95,000 monetary fine would not be justified by retribution and deterrence alone , forfeiture of
petitioner’s airplane is justified by  the goal of preventing its use for  further crimes .
Petitioner errs in suggesting (Br. 32 -37) that all
those differences —and a volume of history besides , see
pp. 9-21, supra—must be disregarded, lest forfeitures go
unchecked.  History would not support the confiscation
of a car involved in a civil traffic violation, such as “going
five miles over the speed limit .”  Pet. Br. 2.  Nor would
history support seizing the lawful cargo in petitioner’s
airplane, or the  airport from which the airplane took off.
See Culley, 601 U.S. at 399 (Gorsuch, J., concurring).
But it does support forfeiture of petitioner’s airplane .
Such forfeiture is accordingly constitutional .

31

CONCLUSION
The judgment of the Supreme Court of Alaska
should be affirmed .
